summary: Gives guidance on developing, deploying and operating DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), which lets an organization take responsibility for a message with a signature checked by the receiver. It uses public-key cryptography and DNS to publish keys. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A sender signs each letter so the receiver can check it came from the company it claims, using a key posted publicly.

subtitle: Practical advice for building, deploying and running DKIM email signing, from key handling to mailing lists.

tldr.problem: DKIM lets a domain sign its mail, but the base specification says little about how to choose signing names, manage keys, or handle forwarders and mailing lists in practice.
tldr.mechanism: This guide explains DKIM as a trust signal: the signer supplies one identifier (d=), the recipient assesses it, and operators follow key, DNS and signing practices that keep that signal meaningful.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational guide rather than a protocol. Its central warning is that a valid DKIM signature shows message integrity and a responsible domain, not that the content or the From address is genuine.

today: RFC 5863 is an Informational document and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains guidance for operators rather than a standard.

sections.title: What DKIM Does and Does Not Prove
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets an organization claim responsibility for transmitting a message in a way that a recipient can validate. This document gives practical advice to people who develop DKIM software, deploy keys, migrate from DomainKeys, and operate mail systems. It suggests reading the DKIM Service Overview (RFC 5585) first.

The guide frames DKIM as a trust mechanism. The signer hands the recipient one identifier, the recipient's Identity Assessor looks up whatever reputation data it has, and a Handling Filter then decides what to do with the message. DKIM validates only that the identifier was legitimately attached to the message. It says nothing about whether the content, or even the RFC5322.From field, is valid. Its only claim about content is that the headers and body covered by the signature were delivered without modification.
sections.eli5: The seal tells you which company stamped the letter and that nobody changed it on the way. It does not tell you the letter is true.

sections.title: Choosing Identifiers and Signing Domains
sections.content:
A signature carries three identification values, but only one is the formal output. The d= tag is the Signing Domain Identifier, a domain name that is also combined with the selector to form a DNS query. The s= tag is the selector, used to tell apart different keys for the same domain. The optional i= tag is the Agent or User Identifier. The guide says the selector should not be used for assessment, because that would leave no way to move from an old or compromised key to a new one. The i= value must be treated as opaque, since it can look like an address yet mean something only the signer knows.

Signers can use different d= subdomains for different mail streams, such as newsletter.example.com or support.example.com, so receivers can judge them separately. Too much granularity makes it hard for a receiver to see a stable pattern, and a receiver that uses only the rightmost part of the name leaves the signer guessing what was assessed.

The guide includes an example grid of Organizational Trust against Stream Risk. Cells are labeled Pristine, Unknown, Malicious, Compromised and so on, each with a suggested handling such as accept, strong filter, block or block and contact.
sections.eli5: The company name on the seal is what matters. Different departments can use slightly different names, but too many names make it hard for anyone to remember who is trustworthy.

sections.title: Keys, DNS and Selectors
sections.content:
In DKIM the public key is published in the DNS, and key distribution and key accreditation are combined. No trusted third party vouches for the key holder. A published key therefore lets a signer claim only that someone who controls the DNS zone intends to take responsibility for messages signed with the matching private key.

For private keys the guide says to keep access to as few key holders as possible, use key management hardware if available, generate the pair close to the signing point, keep a key in exactly one location, and avoid key escrow. Responsibility should rest with a single named individual, and each authorized signer should use a different key. Keeping the key secret matters more than refreshing it often.

On the DNS side, the zone needs the ability to create the records and strong controls against spurious inserts. At a minimum the DNS server must allow free-form TXT records, and DNSSEC is recommended. Selectors are assigned for administrative needs such as key rollover. To retire a key, the signer stops using it, deletes it, and later either publishes an empty p= field or deletes the record. An empty p= acts as a gravestone, making accidental reuse of the selector with a different key less likely.

For third-party signers, the third party should generate the key pair and send only the public key to the domain holder. The domain holder should use least privilege, and may delegate a DNS subzone rather than give unrestricted DNS access.
sections.eli5: Keep the stamp locked up with as few people as possible, and post a public copy of its pattern where anyone can check. When you throw a stamp away, put up a sign saying it is gone.

sections.title: Signing, Verifying and Mail Flow
sections.content:
Signing needs two things: a DNS administrative interface that can handle names including underscores, and a trusted signing module in the outbound mail path that adds the DKIM-Signature: header field. The public key lives at <selector>._domainkey.<domain-name>, initially in TXT records. Signing decisions are best kept in run-time configuration rather than hard-coded.

When verifying, a message whose signature is invalid must be treated as if it were unsigned, no better and no worse. Treating it worse would penalize honest configuration errors, and treating it better would let attackers add junk signatures. A valid signature is only the authentication half of an access decision and must be combined with reputation data. Because it does not prove the key holder kept control of the key or the DNS zone, the DKIM key retrieval is not intended as a high-assurance public key infrastructure for uses such as legally binding contracts.

Mailing lists and other intermediaries often change a message so that the signature fails, so they are strongly encouraged to sign it themselves. Verifiers can pass results along in a results header (RFC 5451), but must protect against bogus ones. Message signers should avoid signing message parts that are likely to be modified. The guide advises against encouraging MUAs to sign, because user machines are more exposed to compromise than a boundary MTA.
sections.eli5: If a seal is broken, treat the letter like one with no seal at all. And if a mailing list opens and rewrites letters, it should add its own seal.

sections.title: Kinds of Signatures and Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The guide sorts signatures by who signs. A single domain signature has the organization signing with its own domain, for example d=companyA.example. An author signature is one whose domain matches the RFC5322.From address. A parent domain signature uses one common parent for several subdomains. A third-party signature has a domain that does not match the From address, such as an email service provider or a reputation provider. The specification gives no special weight to any of these, and most reputation services assign trust to the identifier string rather than to its role.

An organization that outsources mail, such as employee benefits, can have the provider generate a key pair and publish the public key in the organization's DNS, or delegate a subdomain like benefits.companyA.example to the provider. Revoking access means removing the key or the delegation.

A message can carry several signatures, for example one from a sales subdomain and one from the parent domain, or one from a service provider and one from its client. The guide notes there is no clear consensus among receivers on how to handle multiple signatures.

For Author Domain Signing Practices (RFC 5617), the guide warns that publishing a strict policy such as dkim=all or dkim=discardable risks misdelivery of any legitimate mail without a valid author signature. A thorough survey of outbound mail sources is needed first. It also notes that look-alike domains still pass, because DKIM and ADSP only validate the exact identifier.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a shop uses its own seal, sometimes a delivery company seals on its behalf, and sometimes a letter has two seals. Before you promise to throw away every unsealed letter, make sure all your real letters are sealed.

sections.title: Security and Migration Notes
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single sentence pointing to the DKIM base specification (RFC 4871). The guide's own security advice lives in earlier sections, for example the limits of what a valid signature proves: the private key holder might have lost control of the key, the domain holder might have lost control of its DNS server, or ownership of the zone might have changed.

Appendices cover migration strategies, including moving from DomainKeys (RFC 4870), and migrating hash and signing algorithms, followed by general coding criteria for cryptographic applications.
sections.eli5: A good seal still does not prove the stamp was never stolen. The back of the booklet explains how to switch from an old kind of stamp to a newer one.
